record.original_question: For what sets Ω of lattice points (mk , nk ) do the monomials xmk y nk span L2 orPC0 on the unit square 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1? It is conjectured that the condition mk nk = ∞ is sufficient for sets Ω in an angle εx ≤ y ≤ x/ε, ε > 0. Hellerstein [425] has shown that the condition is not necessary. (J. Korevaar)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega = \{(m_k, n_k)\}_{k\ge 1}$ be a set of lattice points in $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2$. Consider the unit square $S = \{(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,\ 0 \le y \le 1\}$, and the family of monomials $\{x^{m_k} y^{n_k}\}_{k \ge 1}$ on $S$.

Characterize those sets $\Omega$ for which the linear span of $\{x^{m_k} y^{n_k}\}$ is dense in $L^2(S)$ (respectively, dense in $C_0(S)$, the space of continuous functions on $S$ vanishing on the union of the coordinate axes intersected with $S$, equipped with the supremum norm).

In particular, assume that $\Omega$ is contained in an angular sector
$$\{(m,n) : \varepsilon m \le n \le m/\varepsilon\}$$
for some $\varepsilon > 0$. Prove or disprove the conjecture that, in this case, the divergence condition
$$\sum_{k} \frac{1}{m_k + n_k} = \infty \quad \text{(equivalently, the Müntz-type condition that } m_k n_k \to \infty \text{ in the appropriate sense)}$$
— more precisely, the condition that "$m_k n_k = \infty$" in the sense given by such a divergence — is sufficient for the monomials to span $L^2(S)$ (or $C_0(S)$).

It is known that this condition is not necessary in general; the question asks for sufficiency within the sector and, more broadly, for a complete characterization of spanning sets $\Omega$.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return specific results addressing the conjecture about completeness of bivariate monomial systems $\{x^{m_k}y^{n_k}\}$ on the unit square within an angular sector. Hellerstein's result that the divergence condition is not necessary is referenced in the original problem, but no source confirming a full resolution of the sufficiency conjecture in the sector $\varepsilon m \le n \le m/\varepsilon$ was located. The status is therefore taken to be unknown.
